title: Pregnancy-Safe Skincare: The Complete Ingredient Avoidance Guide
body_html:
During pregnancy, avoid retinoids, high-percentage salicylic acid, hydroquinone, certain essential oils (in large quantities), and products with endocrine disruptors. Here's the complete ingredient avoidance guide, plus what's actually safe to use and how to build a trimester-by-trimester routine.

This article is informational, not medical advice. Always consult your OBGYN or dermatologist about skincare during your specific pregnancy.

Navigating skincare while pregnant is genuinely confusing. Most safety data on topical ingredients comes from animal studies or extrapolations from oral exposure — not rigorous trials in pregnant humans. The honest answer is that topical absorption is generally low, but "low" isn't zero, and growing a human is not the time for unnecessary risks. This guide gives you a practical, honest framework: what to pause, what's fine to keep, and how to build a routine that supports your skin through each trimester.

Ingredients to Avoid During Pregnancy

Retinoids (retinol, retinyl palmitate, tretinoin, tazarotene)

Retinoids — the vitamin A derivative family — are the most clearly established category to avoid during pregnancy. Oral isotretinoin (Accutane) is a known teratogen, and while topical retinoids have much lower systemic absorption, the established medical consensus is to avoid all retinoid forms during pregnancy and breastfeeding. This includes over-the-counter retinol and retinyl palmitate, prescription tretinoin and adapalene, and stronger tazarotene. The risk from a short, accidental early-pregnancy exposure before you knew you were pregnant is considered low — stop using and let your OBGYN know, but don't panic. The main skincare ingredients to avoid during pregnancy include retinoids at the top of any list.

Looking for alternatives? See our PDRN vs retinol comparison — PDRN is one of the most compelling pregnancy-safe anti-aging options available.

High-Percentage Salicylic Acid (>2%)

Low-concentration salicylic acid (the 0.5–2% range found in many OTC cleansers and toners) is generally considered acceptable for brief, rinse-off use — but high-percentage leave-on formulations, chemical peels, or prolonged use are typically advised against. Salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid that can be absorbed through the skin; high oral doses of salicylates are associated with fetal complications. The precautionary approach: avoid leave-on salicylic acid above 2%, avoid peel-strength concentrations entirely, and opt for glycolic or lactic acid (in low percentages) as gentler alternatives when exfoliation is needed.

Hydroquinone

Hydroquinone is a prescription-strength skin brightener used to treat hyperpigmentation and melasma. It has unusually high dermal absorption — up to 45% of applied hydroquinone can be detected systemically — which makes it one of the more conservative avoidances during pregnancy. Melasma (the "mask of pregnancy") is extremely common and can be frustrating, but hydroquinone is not the right tool during this period. Alternatives: vitamin C, niacinamide, and azelaic acid are all considered safer options for addressing pregnancy-related hyperpigmentation.

Oral and Topical Tetracyclines

Tetracyclines are a class of antibiotics used in some prescription topical acne formulations. They're worth knowing about even though they're rarely found in over-the-counter skincare. During pregnancy, oral tetracyclines are contraindicated due to risks to fetal bone and tooth development; topical forms are typically avoided as well following the same precautionary logic. If you're on a prescription antibiotic topical for acne, speak with your dermatologist and OBGYN about alternatives.

Certain Essential Oils in Excess

Essential oils are potent botanical concentrates — they're not automatically safe because they're "natural." Several essential oils are traditionally flagged as emmenagogues (stimulating uterine contractions) or have insufficient safety data for use in pregnancy, particularly in higher concentrations or prolonged exposure. The list most commonly cited: clary sage, rosemary, basil, cinnamon, sage, and juniper. Lavender and chamomile in low dilutions (under 1%) are generally considered acceptable, but high-concentration aromatherapy or leave-on essential-oil-forward products deserve scrutiny during pregnancy. If a product lists essential oils early in the INCI (indicating higher concentration), that's worth flagging with your care provider.

Endocrine-Disruptor Concerns (Phthalates, Oxybenzone, Some Sunscreen Actives)

This category is more nuanced — "endocrine disruptor" is a mechanism, not a confirmed harm at typical exposure levels, and the science is actively evolving. That said, a pregnancy is a reasonable time to be conservative about known or suspected endocrine-disrupting compounds. Phthalates (often hidden under "fragrance" or "parfum" on ingredient lists) are the most commonly flagged. Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3) is a chemical UV filter with evidence of skin absorption and hormone-disrupting potential — it's the main reason mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) are preferred over chemical filters during pregnancy. Mineral sunscreens are not absorbed into the skin and are consistently rated the safer option in pregnancy guidance from dermatology and obstetric societies.

What's Actually Safe (and Evidence-Based)

The list of what to avoid can feel paralyzing — but there's a solid roster of well-studied ingredients that are considered safe during pregnancy. A genuinely good pregnancy skincare routine is achievable.

  • Hyaluronic acid / sodium hyaluronate: Among the most pregnancy-safe humectants available. Large-molecule HA doesn't penetrate beyond the skin surface; even low-molecular-weight forms have no documented safety concerns in pregnancy. Safe to use freely.
  • Niacinamide: B3 derivative that addresses uneven tone, pores, and barrier function. Well-tolerated, widely studied, no pregnancy contraindications. An excellent alternative to retinol for general skin maintenance.
  • Vitamin C (stable forms): L-ascorbic acid and gentler derivatives like 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid are considered safe. Vitamin C is an antioxidant and mild brightener that helps with pregnancy-related hyperpigmentation without the risks of hydroquinone. Our Vitamin Glow Serum uses 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid — a stabilized, gentler delivery form.
  • Peptides: Signal peptides and structural peptides (including Argireline / Acetyl Hexapeptide-8) are generally considered safe during pregnancy. They're large molecules with low absorption potential and no known risks in available literature.
  • Low-percentage glycolic and lactic acid: AHAs at low concentrations (under 10%) in rinse-off or low-frequency applications are generally accepted as safe. Consult your care provider if you're unsure — many dermatologists are comfortable with periodic low-percentage use.
  • Mineral SPF (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide): The unambiguous best choice for sunscreen during pregnancy. Mineral sunscreens sit on top of the skin and physically reflect UV — they don't absorb into the bloodstream. Preferred over chemical UV filters like oxybenzone and octinoxate.
  • PDRN: Polydeoxyribonucleotide is not on any standard pregnancy-avoidance list for topical actives. PDRN is a large-molecule polynucleotide with no documented systemic absorption risk and an anti-inflammatory mechanism — as opposed to retinoids, which work via cellular receptor modulation. Leaf & Bird's PDRN formulation is vegan-sourced (biotech-synthesized, not salmon-derived), fragrance-free, and formulated without retinoids or hormone-active ingredients. Consult your OBGYN before starting, as with any skincare during pregnancy.
  • Tallow: Ancestral skin nourishment with a lipid profile closely matched to human sebum. Beef tallow is rich in stearic acid, oleic acid, and fat-soluble vitamins — nutrients that support the skin barrier without any synthetic delivery mechanism. Our grass-fed tallow cream is one of the simplest, most ingredient-honest moisturizers available for pregnancy skin.

Trimester-by-Trimester Skin Guidance

First Trimester: Lean Gentle

The first trimester is typically the most turbulent time for skin. Hormone fluctuations — particularly rising progesterone and hCG — can trigger acne, heightened sensitivity, flushing, and unpredictable reactions to products you've used without issue for years. Your skin's tolerance is at its most variable. This is the wrong time to introduce new actives or test high-potency serums.

Recommended approach: strip back to basics. A gentle cleanser, barrier-focused moisturizer (tallow or a simple ceramide formula), and mineral SPF is a complete, defensible routine. If acne is surfacing, azelaic acid (9–15%) is one of the few actives with both pregnancy safety evidence and genuine efficacy against breakouts. Spot-use rather than full-face application minimizes exposure.

Second Trimester: Build Your Routine

Skin often calms significantly in the second trimester. Hormones have leveled out from the first-trimester swings, and many people experience the famed "pregnancy glow" — increased circulation and estrogen creating a more luminous complexion. This is the best window to reintroduce gentle actives and settle into a consistent routine.

Good second-trimester additions: niacinamide (for even tone and pores), low-percentage vitamin C (brightness), hyaluronic acid layers, and peptide serums. If you've been cleared by your OBGYN for PDRN, the PDRN serum is a well-tolerated daily active for anti-aging support during this stable phase.

Third Trimester: Support Stretching Skin

The third trimester brings its own challenges: belly and breast skin stretching rapidly, hormonal shifts again as the body prepares for birth, and skin that may simultaneously be oilier (face) and drier (body). Stretch marks are largely genetic in likelihood, but keeping skin well-hydrated and lipid-nourished is the honest best practice — tallow is excellent here, applied generously to the belly, hips, and thighs. Avoid any products with high essential oil concentrations near term.

Postpartum: Simplest Is Best

After birth, the skin barrier is often compromised and reactive — a combination of hormonal drop, sleep deprivation, and the physiological demands of early breastfeeding. Complicated routines tend to fail at this stage regardless; simple ones get done.

If you're breastfeeding, apply the same general avoidance framework as pregnancy with one additional consideration: skin-to-baby transfer. Products applied to the chest, neck, and hands can transfer to a nursing infant during skin-to-skin contact. This is a particular concern for fragrance-heavy products, which may contain undisclosed sensitizers. Stick to fragrance-free formulas for the first several months, at least near the areas with most infant contact.

Breastfeeding Considerations

The guidance for breastfeeding mirrors pregnancy in most respects: avoid retinoids, use mineral SPF, prefer fragrance-free formulas. The main additional variable is skin-to-infant transfer during nursing. Anything applied to the chest, nipple area, or hands before holding a newborn can reach the infant's skin and mouth. This matters most for fragrances, preservatives at high concentrations, and ingredients with known sensitizing potential.

Specific notes for breastfeeding:

  • Avoid strong synthetic fragrance on the chest and neck when nursing, especially in the newborn period when infant skin barrier function is still developing.
  • Melatonin-containing topical products (a newer category in sleep and anti-aging skincare) have limited safety data for breastfeeding — the conservative approach is to pause these until weaning.
  • High-concentration retinoids should still be avoided for the duration of breastfeeding per most dermatologist and OBGYN guidance, though topical absorption risk is lower than oral intake.
  • If you have a specific ingredient concern about breastfeeding transfer, your pediatrician is the right resource — not just a skincare brand or general internet search.

Most clean, fragrance-free, retinoid-free formulas are appropriate for use during breastfeeding. The Leaf & Bird pregnancy-safe skincare collection was formulated with this life stage in mind.

The Honest Limits of This Guide

We want to be direct about something: pregnancy skincare data is limited across the board. Rigorous clinical trials on topical ingredient safety in pregnant humans are rarely conducted, for obvious ethical reasons. Most guidance is extrapolated from animal studies, oral exposure data, or dermal absorption measurements that may not perfectly predict fetal exposure.

This means two things for you as a consumer:

  1. When an ingredient is flagged as "avoid during pregnancy," it's usually precautionary rather than based on documented human fetal harm. The retinoid warning, for instance, is extremely well-founded based on oral isotretinoin teratogenicity, but the topical retinol risk specifically is more extrapolated.
  2. When an ingredient is listed as "safe," that often means "no documented evidence of harm at typical topical concentrations" — not "definitively proven safe in rigorous pregnancy trials."

Professional consensus (from groups like the American Academy of Dermatology and ACOG) updates over time as data accumulates. The guidance in this article reflects current consensus as of early 2026, but it's not a substitute for a conversation with your OBGYN or dermatologist. Bring your specific products to your appointments — a 30-second INCI review takes little time and gives you actual professional guidance for your specific situation.

FAQ

This article is informational, not medical advice. Always consult your OBGYN or dermatologist about skincare decisions during your specific pregnancy.

Is PDRN safe during pregnancy?

PDRN is generally considered safe during pregnancy. It's a large-molecule polynucleotide with no documented systemic absorption risk through topical application, no known teratogenic effects, and no documented adverse outcomes in available literature. It is not on any standard pregnancy-avoidance list for topical actives. Leaf & Bird's formulation is also vegan-sourced and fragrance-free, removing two common points of concern. That said, individual OBGYN consultation is always recommended before starting any new active during pregnancy — bring the full INCI list to your appointment.

What about phenoxyethanol in skincare during pregnancy?

Phenoxyethanol is one of the most common preservatives in clean-beauty formulations (Leaf & Bird uses it too — full transparency). Current consensus is that phenoxyethanol at approved use levels (up to 1%) is acceptable during pregnancy for external skin application. The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) reviewed it and found it safe at typical concentrations. It's worth knowing it's in your products, but it's not on the must-avoid list for pregnancy at standard use levels.

I used retinol in early pregnancy before I knew — should I be worried?

This is a common and understandably stressful situation. The short answer: stop using retinol immediately, tell your OBGYN, and don't panic. The documented teratogenic risk is from high-dose oral isotretinoin (Accutane), which achieves systemic concentrations far higher than topical retinol. Brief, early-pregnancy topical retinol exposure before pregnancy was confirmed is widely considered a low-risk scenario by dermatologists and OBGYNs — but the right next step is a conversation with your care provider, not further internet research.

What's the safest pregnancy brightening routine?

For pregnancy-safe brightening, the combination of vitamin C (as a stable ester like 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid), niacinamide, and mineral SPF is well-supported and effective. Azelaic acid (a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid) is also considered safe in pregnancy and is specifically effective for melasma. Avoid hydroquinone. A consistent SPF habit may be the single highest-impact brightening intervention during pregnancy — UV exposure is the primary driver of melasma formation and worsening.

Can I keep using essential-oil-based products during pregnancy?

It depends on the oils and the concentration. Low-dilution lavender and chamomile in a leave-on moisturizer are generally considered acceptable. Products front-loaded with rosemary, clary sage, basil, sage, cinnamon, or juniper are the ones to scrutinize. If essential oils are listed in the first half of the INCI (higher concentration), or if you're using essential oils in a home diffuser for extended periods, that's worth discussing with your OBGYN. Products designed for pregnancy with minimal essential oil use are a lower-risk default.

Are "pregnancy-safe" brands actually safer?

Honest answer: "pregnancy-safe" as a label has no regulatory definition. Any brand can use it. The label does signal intent — brands marketing to pregnant people are usually more careful about formulating out retinoids and strong fragrance — but it's not a quality guarantee. Read the INCI. Look for fragrance-free or transparency around specific fragrance ingredients. Confirm no retinoids or hydroquinone. A credible brand should be able to tell you exactly why each ingredient is in the formula. Leaf & Bird publishes full INCIs and formulates without retinoids, without undisclosed fragrance, and without chemical UV filters for all products in our pregnancy-safe collection.
